clue.text: Academic work perhaps secured by boards

definitions.text: Academic work perhaps secured by boards

parts.words: Academic work perhaps secured by boards
parts.note: a scholarly tome is an example of a book, and one bound between stiff covers of board is the sturdier format

explanation.surface: Some scholarly treatise is apparently kept safe by a committee of governors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boards' suggests a governing body; here it is the stiff card covers of a bound book.
explanation.definitionFit: A book with rigid board covers, as opposed to a paperback, is the format named; an academic work is one example.

clue.text: Those with a ring of fire, dammit?

definitions.text: Those with a ring of fire
definitions.meaning: chiming instruments in the infernal regions would ring amid flames

explanation.surface: Someone swears at things that ring with fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A mild oath of exasperation, and literally the chimes found in the inferno.

clue.text: Minister so upstanding, cut short

indicators.note: cut short says the word for upstanding is trimmed back to its opening letters

parts.note: reverend means worthy of respect, and so honourable or upstanding

explanation.surface: A clergyman so honourable that he is interrupted.
explanation.walkthrough: The adjective for venerable is clipped to the usual short title of a clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: The short title used for a clergyman, a minister of religion.

clue.text: Risk admitting a crime — on your head be it!

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so the wager word takes in the rest

parts.note: a bet is a risk or gamble
a sin is a wrongdoing or crime

explanation.surface: A gamble involving an offence, and the blame lands on you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on your head be it' usually puts blame on someone; here it describes a helmet.
explanation.definitionFit: A light medieval steel helmet, worn on the head.

clue.text: Major worth thinking about?

definitions.meaning: read as able to be pondered or weighed up

explanation.surface: An army officer who deserves some thought.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means sizeable or substantial, and broken apart reads as fit to be pondered.

clue.text: A ton, spouse evidently overfed?

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, and a ton is slang for a hundred
hubby is a colloquial word for husband, a spouse

explanation.surface: A partner weighing a ton is plainly eating too much.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is overfed becomes plump, and plump is a synonym for the answer.

clue.text: The rain squally? Get protection overhead

indicators.note: squally weather is gusty and turbulent, so the letters are blown into a new order

explanation.surface: Stormy rain is forecast, so cover your head.
explanation.walkthrough: The protection is not an umbrella but a fine mesh worn to keep hair in place.
explanation.definitionFit: A fine mesh worn over the hair holds a style in place, a light covering for the head.

clue.text: Invention's instant for plant

parts.note: a person's invention or project is their baby, with the possessive kept
a breath is a moment, as in 'in a breath'

explanation.surface: A clever invention produces an instant plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Gypsophila, a garden flower with clouds of tiny white blooms, used in bouquets.

clue.text: Tug, one seen crossing the Atlantic?

definitions.meaning: an American, as seen from Britain across the ocean

explanation.surface: A tugboat spotted making an ocean voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tug' looks like a boat that might cross the ocean; it is a jerk or pull.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden jerk is a pull, and the slang term for an American is the other sense.

clue.text: Go with novels perhaps offering an air of romance?

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters given might instead be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: Reading romantic novels may give one a dreamy, romantic air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals rearranging GO and NOVELS together; 'air' is a tune, not a manner.
explanation.definitionFit: An air is a melody, so a melody about romance is a sentimental ballad of courtship.

clue.text: Parliamentary clanger outside Britain — well, in France

indicators.note: outside says the French word goes round the abbreviation for Britain

parts.note: bien is French for well
GB is the abbreviation for Great Britain

explanation.surface: A political gaffe made abroad, with a shrug of 'well' from France.
explanation.walkthrough: BIG BEN is the great bell in the clock tower of the Houses of Parliament in London; 'clanger' (a blunder) is really a bell.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous bell at Westminster rings out over Parliament, so it is literally a parliamentary bell that clangs.

clue.text: Expected to generate a real number, about a thousand

indicators.note: about places the generated letters around the thousand symbol
generate means produce something new, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: K is the usual abbreviation for a thousand

explanation.surface: A maths instruction to produce a real number of roughly a thousand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to generate' rearranges A REAL NUMBER, and 'about' puts it round K.
explanation.definitionFit: Something expected is ordinary and predictable, so nothing out of the way to note.

clue.text: What may be following on after a good long life?

definitions.text: What may be following on after a good long life?

parts.words: What may be following on after a good long life?
parts.note: in cricket a long life is a good innings, and a side made to follow on bats a second time

explanation.surface: A musing on what comes after a long, well-lived life: an afterlife, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a team forced to 'follow on' bats again straight away; 'a good innings' is British idiom for a long life.
explanation.definitionFit: A team made to follow on must bat its next turn immediately, the batting turn that comes after its first.

clue.text: Lose one's grip — so fail?

definitions.meaning: go wrong or come to grief

explanation.surface: Losing hold of things leads to failure.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means meet with disaster, and literally means become detached.

clue.text: Bird — gawper?

definitions.meaning: a small songbird that takes insects on the wing

explanation.definitionFit: A family of insect-eating birds, and jokingly a slack-jawed starer.

clue.text: Middle of pavement confronted ant

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letters, here the two at the centre of pavement

parts.note: met means encountered or faced, so confronted

explanation.surface: An insect crossing the footpath runs into an ant.
explanation.walkthrough: EMMET is a dialect word for an ant.
explanation.definitionFit: An old dialect word, chiefly English regional, naming the small insect that lives in colonies.

clue.text: After negotiation, relocate fifty on the voting register

indicators.note: negotiation suggests terms reworked, so the letters of relocate are rearranged

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Talks lead to fifty people moving, which affects the list of voters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After negotiation' signals the anagram; 'voting register' reads like the roll itself but is defining an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The register of voters is the roll of the electorate, so anything on it relates to elections.

clue.text: French agreement with Welsh girl in US city state

indicators.note: in places the French and Welsh pieces inside the city's abbreviation

parts.note: LA is Los Angeles
oui is French for yes
Sian is a Welsh girl's name

explanation.surface: A Frenchman and a Welsh girl agree to meet in an American city.
explanation.definitionFit: A US state on the Gulf of Mexico, bought from France in 1803.

clue.text: Presently to embrace me, European individual

indicators.note: embrace means hold within, so the time word wraps around the pronoun

parts.note: soon means presently, in a short while

explanation.surface: A European will shortly hug me.
explanation.definitionFit: An unnamed person, any single human being.

clue.text: Old money flowed into Liverpool, say?

indicators.note: into says the verb's letters go inside the abbreviation

parts.note: Liverpool FC is a football club, so an example of FC (Football Club)
ran means flowed, as a river does

explanation.surface: Cash poured into the city of Liverpool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liverpool' seems to be the city but is the football club, hence FC.
explanation.definitionFit: The French currency before the euro, now a former coin and so an outdated unit of cash.

clue.text: Waste food

definitions.meaning: a piece of fried batter with fruit or meat

explanation.definitionFit: The verb means squander bit by bit; the noun is a battered fried dish.

clue.text: Film Keith suggested?

parts.note: the film's title, run together, carries the name Keith inside it, so the name suggests the title

explanation.surface: A movie recommended by someone called Keith.
explanation.walkthrough: The Marilyn Monroe comedy's title, written out, conceals the name: someli-KEITH-ot.
explanation.definitionFit: A 1959 Billy Wilder comedy starring Marilyn Monroe, so a movie whose letters contain the man's name.

clue.text: Legendary figure making a comeback?

definitions.meaning: the nymph of Greek myth who could only repeat others' words

explanation.definitionFit: The Greek nymph wasted to a voice, and a reflected sound that returns to the hearer.

clue.text: Stroke of genius covering slip

parts.note: a coup is a brilliant, successful move
on means placed upon, so covering

explanation.surface: A brilliant move that hides a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slip' is not an error but a small piece of paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A voucher is a small printed piece of paper, a slip, exchanged for a discount.

clue.text: Ami butch? Terribly unfair

indicators.note: terribly suggests the letters are badly mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone asks, in mock French, whether they look butch, and is told that is unkind.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something excessive or unreasonable, which comes close to unjust.

clue.text: Aussie truck not entirely computerised

indicators.note: not entirely says only part of the word is used, a run from inside it

explanation.surface: An Australian lorry that is only partly run by computer.
explanation.walkthrough: The vehicle is found within compUTErised.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for utility vehicle, the Australian name for a pickup with an open back.

clue.text: Island group, or island around the north

indicators.note: around says the island word wraps round the letter for north

parts.note: a key is a low island or reef, as in the Florida Keys
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: Either an archipelago or a single island in the far north.
explanation.definitionFit: An archipelago off the north-east tip of Scotland.

clue.text: That woman must catch a bird. — I agree!

indicators.note: catch means hold, so the pronoun's letters are split to hold the rest

parts.note: her refers to that woman
a rhea is a large flightless South American bird

explanation.surface: A woman is told she has to catch a bird, and someone approves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must catch' splits the pronoun after its second letter to hold the rest; the cry is the one heard in Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: The cry of approval heard in Parliament and at meetings, used to second what a speaker says.
